<reason>Side A won a closely fought debate through superior comparative weighing. A's core frame — certain, concrete suffering (the ALS patient) versus contested future harms — survived every round, and the Oregon counterexample to B's slope theory was never truly neutralized; B's only rejoinder was that Oregon "hasn't yet finished the litigation," which is itself an admission of speculation. B's strongest line, that conceded principle turns every eligibility line into a discrimination claim, was genuinely powerful and A's answer (Canada-specific Charter logic plus a stable decades-old statute) was adequate but not decisive. B also slightly overreached on grounding by treating "burden on family" survey concerns as "documented" coercion. Both sides handled pressure questions honestly with clean A1/A2 structure; B's evidential-asymmetry answer in B4.1 was excellent, but A's closing — turning B's palliative sedation offer into an autonomy-overriding substitution rather than an answer to the patient's request — was the sharpest single move of the debate and crystallized the choice in A's favor. Minor execution costs for both (clipped opening for A, clipped closing for B).</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange ran through the pressure questions and closings: B answered the ALS patient question by offering palliative sedation to unconsciousness and full refusal rights [B4.3], and A's closing [A5.1] converted that answer into a concession — sedation substitutes someone else's values for her chosen, peaceful death, it does not answer her request. Combined with A's standing point that B never defended the status quo's unregulated harms, this gave A the cleaner terminal comparative frame.</best_rebuttal>
